paragraphs: By SPACE | September 7, 2026 | 10 min read

If you want to sell an ambient or lo-fi music catalog, start by comparing the transaction, not just the company name. SPACE offers direct catalog purchases; Duetti and Limbo also publish acquisition options. Royalty Exchange connects sellers with investors, while beatBread offers royalty advances rather than a conventional catalog buyout. Your rights, earnings and preferred deal structure determine which conversation is relevant.

Disclosure: SPACE publishes this guide and is one of the companies included. This is not an independent ranking or a test of private offers. We compare publicly described services, identify questions to ask and do not claim that any company will accept your catalog or pay the highest price. Sources were checked on September 7, 2026.
In this article

The table separates potential acquisition routes from funding alternatives. It does not imply that every company specializes in ambient or lo-fi, or that an advance transfers the underlying copyright.

Primary Wave is included for wider market context, not as a verified small-catalog application route. The other entries offer more directly described catalog-sale or funding processes. Inclusion is not confirmation of genre-specific eligibility.

SPACE buys catalogs directly from independent artists, producers, labels and owners. There is no application charge, listing fee or auction commission. The review considers the rights and revenue evidence, and sellers are not obliged to accept an offer. SPACE's offer policy.

An initial offer typically takes 5-7 business days after the relevant catalog information is received, subject to review. Payment follows completion of the agreement and transfer requirements; that review estimate is not a guaranteed payment deadline. Timing and payment policy.

When to consider it: You want a private purchase discussion rather than running an auction. For the genre-specific application context, see selling an ambient catalog or selling a lo-fi beats catalog.

What to check: Ask which recordings, ownership shares and income streams are included. A direct process does not guarantee an offer, a premium price or the absence of continuing contractual obligations.

Duetti publicly offers purchases of master, publishing and royalty interests, alongside catalog management and marketing. Its website also describes deals for contributors with royalty income who do not control the master. Duetti's services and purchase scope.
When to consider it: You want to discuss an acquisition and the management of the catalog after the transaction.

What to check: Confirm the interest being purchased, any retained income, required distribution arrangements and which services form part of the signed agreement. Published services are not a guarantee of higher future royalties or acceptance of your catalog.

Limbo describes catalog sales covering masters, publishing, or both, from individual tracks to full or partial interests. It says it works with professional investor partners, rather than describing itself simply as a standalone acquisition fund. Limbo's catalog-sale page.

Its advance offering has an important qualification: Limbo says royalty advances are exclusive to its distribution clients. The advance is recouped from a share of royalties, with terms and cost agreed per deal. Limbo's advance conditions.
When to consider it: You want to explore sale structures, or you already distribute through Limbo and want to discuss an advance.

What to check: Identify the contracting purchaser or funding party. Ask whether distribution migration, administration or other arrangements are required for the specific product you are considering. An illustrative multiple on a website is not your offer.

Royalty Exchange's auction process allows a seller to define the royalty asset and minimum starting price. If that price is not met, no sale occurs. The listing agreement identifies the asset and platform fee, and the process includes verification of royalty records. Royalty Exchange's seller process.
When to consider it: You want to test investor demand through a marketplace rather than negotiate only with a single purchaser.

What to check: Ask what appears in the listing, who can access earnings information, what the fee covers and when payment becomes available. Competitive bidding may help, but there is no basis here for predicting that it will outperform or underperform a private offer for your catalog.

beatBread says its advances are not loans and describes them as purchases of a limited portion of revenues for a limited time. It charges fees but says it does not charge interest. Its FAQ also explains that collections can continue beyond the term if the advance has not recouped. beatBread's FAQ.
When to consider it: You want capital and are willing to share future revenues rather than pursue a conventional full catalog sale.

What to check: Compare the amount advanced, fees, retained income, included tracks, future-release commitments and recoupment conditions. Do not assume that every advance is cost-free, that all royalties are withheld, or that all providers use the same legal structure.

Primary Wave's public positioning emphasizes iconic catalogs and artist or estate partnerships, with investment, marketing and catalog development. Its history includes varied rights transactions, not just one standardized form of buyout. Primary Wave's company overview.
When to consider it: You are assessing whether a broader catalog or artist partnership fits its strategy, potentially with professional representation.

What to check: Establish acquisition fit before using major public deals as a valuation comparison. We have not verified a universal minimum deal size or a rule excluding all independent, ambient or lo-fi catalogs. We therefore do not label it either universally accessible or categorically unavailable.

A catalog used for study, sleep or meditation should be assessed on its own records. A genre label does not prove predictable earnings, and a long track list does not establish diversification if a handful of recordings generates most of the income.
Prepare evidence that helps explain:

Do not treat a public stream count as equivalent to cash received. Spotify says confirmed artificial streaming can lead to withheld royalties and corrected public counts, and warns against paid third parties guaranteeing streams or playlist placement. Spotify's artificial-streaming guidance.

Genre familiarity can make the conversation more relevant. It does not establish that a specialist will always pay more than a diversified buyer. Ask each counterparty how it evaluates the documented income and risks rather than assuming its branding predicts the price.
Give each prospective buyer the same proposed rights scope and the same revenue records. Then compare the written responses using a consistent checklist:
For worked arithmetic and a fuller net-proceeds checklist, read our lump-sum catalog sale guide. It deliberately labels sample multiples as assumptions rather than market offers.
Before committing, have independent legal and tax advisers review the actual agreement. This comparison is general information, not personalized financial, tax or legal advice.

An application response, a conditional offer and money available in your bank account are different milestones. Ask each provider for a timeline that separates them rather than comparing an advertised review period with another company's full closing process.

A direct buyer avoids an auction stage, but that alone does not prove it will pay sooner. Royalty Exchange's seller process, for example, releases funds after the transfer is complete, not simply when bidding ends. Royalty Exchange's closing process.

Request an itemized explanation of the costs payable at application, listing, withdrawal and closing. Do not assume an auction charges the same fees whether or not an asset sells, or that a free application makes every eventual transaction cost disappear. Compare net proceeds after the deductions that actually apply to your agreement.

A sale is not automatically a release from every obligation. Check ownership warranties, cooperation requirements, licensing approvals and the reporting needed for any interest you retain. An upfront payment describes when money arrives; it does not, by itself, establish the duration or scope of the deal.
No route is automatically best for every producer. Our partial versus full sale comparison can help you define the interest you want reviewed.

This guide cannot establish a highest-paying company from public marketing pages. Compare actual offers for the same rights and income. A higher headline price may include a larger interest, a longer term or less favorable conditions.

No. Royalty Exchange operates a marketplace, while beatBread's described funding product is an advance structured as a revenue purchase. Limbo offers both sales and advances with different conditions. Confirm the counterparty and transaction before comparing proposals.

No. Ask the provider to distinguish what happens when royalties underperform from what happens if a contractual promise is breached. Review the revenue-sharing term, fees, reporting and any exceptions with your adviser. Also confirm whether collections end at recoupment, at the end of the term, or only when both conditions are met; do not assume these are the same date.

We have not established a universal genre-specific market range. A multiple only becomes comparable once the earnings definition, ownership share, term and included rights match. Website illustrations and celebrity acquisitions do not establish an offer for your catalog.

Yes, if you own those publishing interests and the transaction leaves them outside the sale. Recording and composition rights are separate. Make the retained rights explicit; our masters versus publishing comparison explains the distinction.

Not if the agreement is expressly limited to specified existing works and contains no relevant future-release commitment or option. Do not rely on a marketing summary: check the contract's scope before assuming future music is excluded.

Gather your royalty statements and ownership records, decide what you would consider selling, and ask for the terms in writing. If you want SPACE to review your catalog, apply for a free catalog evaluation. You can also estimate your catalog value as an indicative starting point, not a guaranteed offer.
